question:
A 44-year-old female patient comes to the office reporting intermittent headaches for the past 6
months. She describes a dull pain typically localized at the skull base, with minimal relief from
ibuprofen. Her history includes a minor head injury from a skiing accident one year prior. She reports
no visual disturbances, nausea, or vomiting. Neurological examination reveals no focal deficits. During
cranial vault hold examination, the examiner notes that on the right side, the index and little fingers
spread apart and move downward, while on the left side, the index and little fingers converge and move
upward. Which cranial strain pattern most likely explains these findings? Answer Choices: (A) Cranial
base compression (B) Sphenobasilar flexion (C) Sphenobasilar extension (D) Lateral strain (E) Left
torsion (F) Right sidebending and rotation (G) Right torsion (H) Vertical strain (I) Inferior vertical strain
(J) Left sidebending and rotation
 A. Sphenobasilar flexion
B. Sphenobasilar extension
C. Vertical strain
D. Left torsion
E. Lateral strain

F. Inferior vertical strain
G. Right sidebending and rotation
H. Right torsion
I. Cranial base compression
J. Left sidebending and rotation
